title: Pauri 40, meaning: hear the bliss
hookLine: hear the song of bliss, fortunate ones; all longings are fulfilled (Anand 40)

lines: CROSS ONE OFF, TWO MORE APPEAR.
LISTEN, LUCKY ONES: ALL LONGINGS MET.
cards: A sticky note on the fridge, a list of things wanted. A job. A test result.
A phone call from someone. A child who sleeps through the night. Cross one off and two more get added underneath.
Then someone calls out across a crowded hall: listen, you lucky ones, every one of those longings is met. That's how the last pauri of the Anand begins.

teach.h: HEAR THE BLISS, YOU FORTUNATE ONES.
teach.b: Here's the first line, in paraphrase. Anad sunahu: hear the bliss. Vaddabhaageeho: you of great fortune.
Sagal manorath poore: all longings are fulfilled. Then the pauri says how.

teach.h: THE LORD FOUND, EVERY ANXIETY GONE.
teach.b: The Supreme Lord has been found, and every anxiety is gone. Pain, sickness and suffering leave, it says, by hearing the true bani.
The saints and friends are delighted, because they've come to know it through the perfect Guru. Then a line that echoes a pauri we heard nine days ago.

teach.h: PURE ARE THE HEARERS, HOLY THE SPEAKERS.
teach.b: Back in pauri twenty-four, unripe were the speakers and unripe the hearers. Here, at the end, it flips: pure are those who hear, holy are those who speak, and the True Guru fills everything.
The Anand closes with Nanak's prayer, at the Guru's feet, and a sound: the unstruck music, anahad, playing on and on, like trumpets nobody is blowing.
So what does every longing met mean? Not that the list gets checked off. The pauri is sung by people who still have bills, illnesses and phone calls that don't come.
The pauri says the longings are fulfilled because the One they were all reaching for has been found. The list was a long way of wanting one thing.
Some Sikhs hear in this why the Anand is sung at the close of every gathering: whatever the occasion was about, the song ends where all the longings end. Every longing met.

how: The fortieth pauri is sung with the first five at the close of Sikh services and ceremonies, and is the last pauri of the full Anand Sahib that many Sikhs recite each morning.

o: a vow made at the gurdwara's door
a written list of duties for the day
a longing, a wish the heart reaches for

s: pauri forty says the hearers and speakers are pure
the reverse of pauri 24, where both were unripe.
every longing met means everything on your list gets checked off
the pauri says longings are fulfilled because the One they reached for is found.
it ends with the unstruck music, anahad, playing on.

games.q: pauri 24 said unripe are the speakers and unripe the hearers. what does pauri 40 say about them?
o: pure are the hearers, holy are the speakers.
games.why: at the end of the Anand it flips: hearing the true bani, the hearers and speakers are made pure.

practice: If you can find a recording of the six pauris, play the last one, from anad sunahu to the end, and let it pass through you; if not, sit with its first line.
Bring one longing from your list to mind and set it gently beside the line, not to cancel it, just to see it in that light. Then breathe.

wordCard.voice: Manorath, a longing. The last pauri of the Anand: hear the bliss, fortunate ones, all manorath are fulfilled; pure are the hearers, holy the speakers; the unstruck music plays.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: manorath, a longing, a heart's wish; in pauri 40, sagal manorath poore: all longings fulfilled.

carryVoice: Your line: every longing met. The list may stay on the fridge; the song is sung anyway. Until tomorrow.
